title: Pinch-pot cactus planter
subtitle: A small rounded pot for a single succulent or cactus, with a drainage hole
excerpt: A pinch pot is the right form for a small cactus planter: rounded sides, a drainage hole in the base, and walls thick enough to hold their shape during drying without a mould. This version uses air-dry clay and a layer of waterproofing sealant inside so moisture from watering does not collapse the pot. Holds a 5 cm nursery pot or a small succulent direct.
sourceNotes: Pinch-pot technique derived from first principles. Small planter form derived from traditional domestic ceramics.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried but unfired clay. Fragile; the final stage before sealing an air-dry piece.
A hand-built clay form made by pressing the thumb into a ball of clay and pinching the walls outward to shape a hollow vessel.

content.text: Air-dry clay suits a cactus planter well. Cacti dry out between waterings, so the pot is not under constant wet stress. This is different from a herb pot, which stays damp. The clay needs three things: a drainage hole in the base, walls thick enough to dry without cracking, and three coats of sealant on the inside before you plant anything.
What you'll need
Around 150 g of air-dry clay for a pot roughly 8 cm across and 7 cm tall. Target wall thickness: 6 to 8 mm throughout.
Forming the pot

Roll 150 g of air-dry clay into a smooth ball between both palms. Knead for two minutes to ensure even moisture throughout. If the surface shows cracks when bent, the clay is too dry: work in a few drops of water with the palms and knead again.
Press the thumb of one hand into the centre of the ball, stopping 8 mm from the base. Do not push all the way through. The pot should be closed at the bottom: the base will be pierced later.

Pinch the walls outward: press the thumb from inside against two fingertips on the exterior, rotating the ball a quarter-turn between each pinch. Keep pinches even and close together: large pinch marks leave thin spots between thick ones.

After two full circuits of pinching, check the wall thickness by feeling between thumb and finger. Aim for 6 to 8 mm. Where walls are thicker than 8 mm, pinch more firmly. Where walls are thinner than 6 mm, avoid that area and build up thickness from the outside by adding a small piece of clay and blending it in.
Pat the base of the pot flat against the work surface so it stands upright without rocking. The base should be 7 to 8 mm thick.

Pierce a drainage hole through the centre of the base with the needle tool. Make it 6 to 8 mm in diameter: the hole will shrink slightly as the clay dries. Widen the needle-tool hole by rotating the tool in a circle.
Smooth the rim with a dampened fingertip. Smooth the exterior surface with the wooden rib. Leave any finger marks you prefer as texture.
Drying
Set the pot upright on a smooth tile. Leave uncovered at room temperature for 24 hours. Because the walls are thick, the pot takes longer to dry than a thin
pinch pot
: it is
bone-dry
when it has lightened in colour evenly and feels cool but not cold to the touch.
Finishing

Apply three coats of acrylic sealant to the interior, extending over the rim and 1 cm down the exterior at the rim. This seals the most likely water contact points. Apply two coats to the exterior. Allow each coat to dry fully. Sit the pot on a small saucer to catch any drainage water.
Care

Water sparingly and allow the potting medium to dry completely between waterings: air-dry clay planters are not suited to plants that need constant moisture. The sealant protects the clay from occasional watering but not from sustained damp. Replace or reseal the planter if the interior sealant shows signs of wear.
Variations
Press a texture into the exterior wall: a woven cloth, a fork, or a pressed leaf: before the clay starts to stiffen.
Make three pots in graduated sizes and arrange them as a set on a tray.
Build in paper-clay-air-dry for stronger joins and less risk of rim cracking.

rows.cause: Rim pinched too thin; dried too fast
rows.fix: Keep the rim wall at least 5 mm thick. If a crack appears while still leather-hard, press it closed and smooth with a dampened fingertip.

rows.problem: Drainage hole closes up or narrows severely as clay dries
rows.cause: Normal clay shrinkage; hole pierced too small
rows.fix: Pierce the hole to at least 8 mm diameter while fresh. If the dried hole is too small, enlarge it carefully with a small drill bit on the dry clay.

rows.cause: Base too thin; or pot dried on a surface that caused uneven drying
rows.fix: Keep the base at least 7 mm thick. Dry on a smooth tile, not on cloth which can grip and prevent even shrinkage.
